Proto-Hellenic *gignṓskō Ancient Greek γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō) Proto-Indo-European *-mṓ Ancient Greek -μων (-mōn) Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn)bor. Etruscanbor.? Latin norma Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālis Latin nōrmālisder. English normal English abnormal From ab- + normal.

senses.d: Not conforming to rule or system; deviating from the usual or normal type.
ex: And then after an abnormal meal, which was either a very late breakfast or a very early lunch, they drove on to Victoria Station.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to that which is irregular, in particular, behaviour that deviates from norms of social propriety or accepted standards of mental health.
A person or object that is not normal.

grp.label: not conforming to rule or system
of or pertaining to behaviour that deviates from norms

fr:hors norme.gl: abnormal, unusual, out of the ordinary

ety.text: From Late Latin anōmalus, anōmalos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos, “uneven, irregular”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin anormālis, variant of anormalus, corruption of anōmalus by confusion with norma (“norm, standard”).
Borrowed from French anormal, from Latin anōrmālis. By surface analysis, a- + normal.
